searchText: for the launchpad website, there's a checklist and in the checklist there's a suggestion to turn on ntp on ubuntu 20.04 systems i believe (if my understanding is correct), that is not sufficient to continiously keep your clock in sync. You'd need to install ```chrony``` to do what ntpd normally does not sure if anyone here is involved in 'beaconscan.com', but a couple of times now its reported that the finalized epoch is 1 behind head, which is probably unlikely... https://beaconscan.com/ > not sure if anyone here is involved in 'beaconscan.com', but a couple of times now its reported that the finalized epoch is 1 behind head, which is probably unlikely... https://beaconscan.com/ <@!680234424037670912> They are pretty responsive to messages posted in the block explorers channel of the ethstaker discord But I do see <@!213279392275628032> is in this discord as well ok thanks 🙂 I'm not on that atm, but i think i've got another message for them too, so i'll find it thanks for the tag <@!695019898274840626>! <@!680234424037670912> thanks for bringing it up, will check with the team. we've been having issues catching up since non-finality started, may or may not be related possibly it got the 2 values from different states? im not sure, but i'd be curious if 1 state had the finalized only +1 epoch, its unusual Yet another case where having a dedicated FFG viewer would make it a lot easier to see what happened, especially after the fact Why is `EPOCHS_PER_ETH1_VOTING_PERIOD` `64` instead of say `1` epoch? Because you wouldn't want a very small set of proposers to collude and make a bad majority vote go in so quickly. Fork choice can technically avoid such events, but avoiding such situation altogether is better. do validators attesting to a block not check that the eth1 root is valid? According to the fork choice spec: > Eth1 data: The large ETH1_FOLLOW_DISTANCE specified in the honest validator document should ensure that state.latest_eth1_data of the canonical Ethereum 2.0 chain remains consistent with the canonical Ethereum 1.0 chain. If not, emergency manual intervention will be required. That distance, and a large majority vote, is what the spec describes. ah i see, so it's just the proposers who are voting on the canonical eth1 root -- attesters just disregard the proposers vote when running the fork choice? And honest validators would not be able to build on a bad majority vote, since they cannot include the claimed deposits. Such chain should stall, and get forked out. Not my design however, so I may be missing other key points makes sense, thanks <@!203220829473996800> 🙂 > And honest validators would not be able to build on a bad majority vote, since they cannot include the claimed deposits. <@!203220829473996800> why can't they include the claimed deposits? if there is some malicous deposit root voted in, the honest validators would simply not recognize it. And proposers are forced to include deposits in order, if we know they exist based on the previous majority vote. So such bad deposit chain should stay (almost, except rare attacker proposal) empty This is more of a "what if", after a hypothetical attack though. In reality I expect the follow distance and vote period to do its work. And if not, it's a special thing, we fork it out manually, and increase the voting period until we decide on a better solution. <@!543900561460822016> I personally think that makes sense to disregard bad branches (wrt bad eth1data votes in blocks) in all validators' (and any node following the eth1 chain as well as the beacon chain) fork choice, which would significantly tighten up the security of this component The main reason it's not in the spec is because I've failed to carve out the time to put it there. At this point, I want to check with clients on complexity before pushing for it. Good thing is taht fork choice can be tightened up in this way without a hard fork or major version bump

excerpts.author: lightclient
excerpts.content: Why is `EPOCHS_PER_ETH1_VOTING_PERIOD` `64` instead of say `1` epoch?

excerpts.author: protolambda
excerpts.content: Because you wouldn't want a very small set of proposers to collude and make a bad majority vote go in so quickly. Fork choice can technically avoid such events, but avoiding such situation altogether is better.

excerpts.author: lightclient
excerpts.content: do validators attesting to a block not check that the eth1 root is valid?

excerpts.author: protolambda
excerpts.content:
According to the fork choice spec:
> Eth1 data: The large ETH1_FOLLOW_DISTANCE specified in the honest validator document should ensure that state.latest_eth1_data of the canonical Ethereum 2.0 chain remains consistent with the canonical Ethereum 1.0 chain. If not, emergency manual intervention will be required.

excerpts.author: protolambda
excerpts.content: That distance, and a large majority vote, is what the spec describes.

excerpts.author: lightclient
excerpts.content: ah i see, so it's just the proposers who are voting on the canonical eth1 root -- attesters just disregard the proposers vote when running the fork choice?

excerpts.author: protolambda
excerpts.content: And honest validators would not be able to build on a bad majority vote, since they cannot include the claimed deposits. Such chain should stall, and get forked out. Not my design however, so I may be missing other key points

excerpts.author: lightclient
excerpts.content: makes sense, thanks <@!203220829473996800>  🙂

excerpts.author: sacha6557
excerpts.content:
> And honest validators would not be able to build on a bad majority vote, since they cannot include the claimed deposits. 
<@!203220829473996800> why can't they include the claimed deposits?

excerpts.author: protolambda
excerpts.content: if there is some malicous deposit root voted in, the honest validators would simply not recognize it. And proposers are forced to include deposits in order, if we know they exist based on the previous majority vote. So such bad deposit chain should stay (almost, except rare attacker proposal) empty

excerpts.author: protolambda
excerpts.content: This is more of a "what if", after a hypothetical attack though. In reality I expect the follow distance and vote period to do its work. And if not, it's a special thing, we fork it out manually, and increase the voting period until we decide on a better solution.

excerpts.author: djrtwo
excerpts.content: <@!543900561460822016> I personally think that makes sense to disregard bad branches (wrt bad eth1data votes in blocks) in all validators' (and any node following the eth1 chain as well as the beacon chain) fork choice, which would significantly tighten up the security of this component

excerpts.author: djrtwo

At this point, I want to check with clients on complexity before pushing for it.

Good thing is taht fork choice can be tightened up in this way without a hard fork or major version bump
